rv.q: What marked them out was their compassionate depiction of dignity and care in the face of hardship: I will never forget the man in Love tenderly washing his elderly mother’s hair in the kitchen sink of their temporary accommodation.
It's quietly touching and hugely life-affirming.
The result is absorbing, an immersion in detail that has something in common with the work of the American dramatist Annie Baker: it is as if you are seeing all the individual pixels in a photograph.
Never before has a nude scene felt so sober, so grimly unprurient, and Zeldin – who directs as well – takes command of a difficult moment with subtlety and sympathy.
This is simply a presentation of one existence, albeit so beautifully crafted it can’t help but sting.
The Confessions needs your patience, but it rewards it.
If The Confessions doesn’t quite offer the same sense of audience communion as Zeldin’s previous work, as a gesture it is moving.
Theatre Lyttelton’s stage currently conveys places and situations pivotal in the life experience of one particular Australian woman.
He has fashioned it into a fine, uplifting tribute that portrays the heroism of “ordinary” people with a warm wit and breadth of understanding.
It is compelling throughout in its telling of the story of an “ordinary” woman whose life and achievements have been anything but.
Stay at home. Watch bark grow. It’s more exciting than this vanity project.

cn.t: Zeldin's deeply personal drama tracing an ordinary Australian woman's life across decades draws mostly strong praise for its unsentimental humanity and hyper-real dialogue, though some find it interminable and pointless.
